## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds, so it gives no gradient to follow. Under the default recipe, the 131k-step budget comes to only about 32 PPO updates of 4096 samples. That is probably too few to learn exact builds, so the recipe may be part of the bottleneck. The task's core perception problem is this: for each brick type and anchor, find the landing layer (the maximum build height under the footprint) and check that the target is missing exactly those cells at that layer. The starting network mixes all layers through 1x1 convolutions, which makes this layer lookup hard. This round separates two factors. One trial changes only the recipe (fewer epochs, smaller batches, more updates, lower entropy). The other two test a layer-conditioned network that scores every (type, anchor, layer) and reduces over layers, under two recipes.

### Round 2
All three trials scored 0 on dev, and training success was also 0 in the last 10% of every run. So neither the recipe change nor the layer-conditioned scorer has been tested in a regime where the agent learns anything. Likely causes:
(a) Too few samples or updates. With 1 PPO epoch the budget allows about 426k steps at r≤1, and this has not been tried with a large n_envs.
(b) The agent may collapse to choosing DONE early. Random placements mostly give negative reward, so ending the episode looks better. A lower entropy coefficient (r1c1 to r1c3 used 0.003) and gamma 0.95 could make this worse.
(c) The task note warns the world may differ from its description. If so, the fixed footprint-pooling heads, which assume a top-left anchor, could be misaligned.
This round uses one shared recipe: 1 epoch, 256 envs, lr 1.5e-3, entropy 0.01, gamma 0.99, lambda 0.95. Under it I compare the starting network as a control, a layer-conditioned network with a learned 3x3 type head, and a deeper 2D network with a learned 3x3 type head.

### Round 3
All six trials scored 0 on dev and 0 on training success. That covers the starting net, layer-conditioned scorers, learned 3x3 heads and recipes from 1 to 2 epochs with up to 405k steps. Two things stand out. First, the round 1–2 recipes gave fewer gradient steps (about 1.6k–1.8k) than the default (about 4.1k), so optimisation may have been starved. Second, with many legal placements and mostly negative rewards for random bricks, PPO may collapse onto an early DONE. That fits zero training success. Architecture changes did nothing so far. This round tests: (1) many small minibatch updates plus a near-uniform starting policy; (2) the same setup with stronger exploration and a shorter horizon against early DONE; (3) a new idea, global attention over columns, so the DONE decision and placements can see the whole design.

### Round 4
All 9 trials scored exactly 0 on dev and 0 on training success. That held across three trunk families (column CNN, per-layer shared net, column transformer), fixed-pooling and learned 3x3 heads, and recipes from 1 to 2 epochs, 120k to 405k steps, entropy 0.003 to 0.03 and gamma 0.9 to 0.99. When every recipe and architecture fails identically, the likely cause is something every trial shared. All of them map logits to actions with spatially aligned conv heads, each type's map indexed by (y, x) from the top-left anchor. The task warns that the world may not behave as described. If the action indexing, the anchor convention or the footprint order differs from the description, no conv-aligned head can learn the policy. My guess is that this mismatch is the bottleneck. In this last round I test dense action heads that can learn any mapping from index to placement, ranging from a conv trunk with a dense head to a pure MLP.
